piano.ambientazione: Cedar Hollow, a small town in the Vermont hills, present day. The story unfolds during the week leading up to the town's beloved annual Founder's Day Festival in early autumn.
atti: Maggie Doyle, new owner of her late mother's bakery, discovers the Founder's Day Committee president dead in her proofing drawer on festival morning, and a recipe card in his pocket written in her deceased mother's hand makes Maggie the police's prime suspect.

Determined to clear her name, Maggie digs into her mother's old coded recipes and the festival's finances, uncovering a years old embezzlement scheme and mounting evidence that her mother's death three years earlier was no accident, until a piece of planted false evidence nearly destroys her and her business.

Armed with proof from a storage unit, a torn ledger, and her mother's final warning, Maggie helps expose committee treasurer Denise Cobb as the killer of both Harold and Rose during a tense confrontation at the festival's closing ceremony, finally restoring her mother's name and securing the bakery's future.

capitoli.cosa_succede: Maggie arrives before dawn to start the festival bread order and finds Harold Pruitt's body slumped against her bakery's open proofing drawer, ruined dough spilling over his shoulder. She calls 911, and Deputy Nate Coleman arrives first, sealing off her kitchen hours before the festival is set to open.

Chief Bill Torres questions Maggie in her own dining room while forensic techs bag evidence from the kitchen she just spent her savings renovating. He shows her a stained recipe card pulled from Harold's coat pocket and asks her to confirm the handwriting is her mother's, watching her face closely when she does.

News of the recipe card spreads through Cedar Hollow by breakfast, and Ruth Ann Sawyer volunteers to supply the festival's baked goods in Maggie's place. That night Maggie and Josie tape brown paper over the windows to block out gawkers, and Maggie notices one card missing from her mother's recipe box, one she cannot remember ever being pulled.

Maggie and Josie go through the recipe box card by card and find faint pencil numbers in the margins of a dozen cards, all dated the month before Rose died. Nate stops by off duty to warn Maggie that the state police may get involved, and he lingers long enough to notice the numbers himself.

At Harold's wake in the Grange hall, Maggie steels herself to pay respects and ends up seated beside his widow, Diane, who is oddly candid in her grief. Diane tells her that Harold had been distracted for weeks, slipping out at night to meetings he refused to explain.

Maggie visits the Founder's Day Committee office to retrieve paperwork for her canceled festival contract and finds treasurer Denise Cobb unusually solicitous, while developer Walter Finch reviews land papers at the next desk. Denise snaps a ledger shut the moment Maggie's eyes drift toward it, waving off the reaction as embarrassment over unrelated committee debts.

Nate meets Maggie quietly behind the bakery to tell her the county coroner ruled Harold's head wound inconsistent with a simple fall, making the case an official homicide. He also mentions a technician found the faint pressed impression of a second, more recent hand on the back of the recipe card, as if someone had written on a sheet resting on top of it.

Using the heat lamp from the proofing cabinet and a soft pencil, Maggie and Josie coax the hidden impression on the recipe card into legibility and read a fragment about the Grange numbers not adding up. Chief Torres, fed rumors by Ruth Ann about Maggie's temper and motive, publicly names her a formal suspect, and Maggie decides she will find the truth herself before the town decides it for her.

With her kitchen released back to her under police condition, Maggie reopens the bakery to a town split between loyal regulars and wary strangers, while Josie mans the register and fields whispered questions. That evening the two women dig through old Founder's Day financial records at the town library and uncover a controversial rezoning vote from three years earlier tied to Walter Finch's stalled development.

Maggie corners Ruth Ann Sawyer about the gossip she has been spreading and gets a defensive, almost comic confession that it was jealousy over the bakery and nothing more sinister. Flustered, Ruth Ann blurts out that she saw Harold's car parked at the Grange hall very late the night before he died, a detail she had been too embarrassed to mention.

Maggie convinces Nate to walk through the Grange hall with her after hours, where they find chairs still arranged for a hushed late meeting and two cold, uncleared coffee cups. In the trash bin behind the building they find a torn ledger page whose numbers match the code from Rose's recipe cards exactly.

Maggie returns to see Diane Pruitt and gently lays out what she and Nate have found, and Diane's composure finally cracks. She admits she has been too afraid to look at Harold's credit card statements and hands over a bill for a storage unit rental she never knew he had.

Maggie and Josie open the rented unit and find boxes of old Founder's Day financial records alongside a spare key to Rose's old bakery labeled in Harold's own handwriting. Tucked beneath it is a sympathy card, never sent, that reads like a confession of guilt toward a family he never dared face.

With Nate's help, Maggie requests her mother's old medical file and learns Rose had no history of heart trouble before the attack that supposedly killed her. That night someone breaks into the closed bakery and tears through the recipe box without touching the register, leaving Maggie certain the truth about her mother's death has just become dangerous.

Chief Torres dismisses the break-in as random vandalism despite the untouched cash drawer, and Nate's insistence that it is connected puts him at odds with his own boss for the first time. Sorting through the scattered cards afterward, Maggie realizes the one card with the coded numbers is the only one actually gone.

Maggie visits the retired town pharmacist, who still keeps old records, and learns that Rose's blood pressure medication could have been altered to trigger a fatal reaction with no one the wiser. The pharmacist recalls that only a small circle of committee friends ever had reason to be alone in Rose's kitchen those last weeks, and Denise Cobb's name comes up first.

At a public Founder's Day meeting held despite the murder, Denise pushes the committee to move past these distractions and finish the festival, growing visibly rattled when a councilman raises the stalled rezoning deal. Afterward a cornered Walter Finch warns Maggie in the parking lot to stop digging before more people get hurt, a warning that sounds like fear rather than threat.

An anonymous tip delivers Chief Torres a forged note supposedly in Rose's hand implicating Maggie in an old grudge against Harold, and Maggie is hauled in for formal questioning while Nate is reprimanded for helping her. Released without charges but publicly humiliated, Maggie watches two festival vendors cancel their standing bakery orders and wonders, for the first time since coming home, if she should simply sell the bakery and leave.

Grieving and ready to quit, Maggie is visited by her mother's old friend and former schoolteacher, who finally shares a letter Rose wrote weeks before she died, warning that D was the real danger on the committee, not Harold. The letter restores Maggie's resolve, and she and Nate agree the evidence now points squarely at Denise Cobb.

Wary of Chief Torres, Maggie and Nate quietly bring their evidence, the ledger fragment, the storage unit contents, and Rose's coded cards, to a state investigator willing to listen. Together they plan to flush Denise into the open during the festival's closing ceremony, where Maggie is scheduled to unveil the Founder's Day cake in front of the whole town.

On the festival's final afternoon, Maggie performs her public duty at the cake ceremony while plainclothes officers watch the crowd, and Denise finds her alone backstage afterward under the guise of concern. Fishing for what Maggie truly knows, Denise lets slip a detail about exactly how Harold's body had been positioned in the proofing drawer, a detail never released to the public.

Realizing her mistake, Denise turns cold and forces Maggie back into the bakery's kitchen, locking the door and admitting she killed Harold to stop his confession and, years earlier, tampered with Rose's medication to silence her. Josie notices Maggie's absence from the crowd and alerts Nate, who breaks the kitchen door open with backup seconds after Denise raises a heavy rolling pin against Maggie.

With Denise in custody, Walter Finch cooperates fully with investigators to avoid charges, laying out years of skimmed festival funds funneled into his failed development, and Chief Torres is forced to publicly admit he pursued the wrong suspect from the start. Maggie is formally cleared, and the town's shock at Denise's arrest gives way to a quiet, collective reckoning with how long the truth about Rose had gone unspoken.

Weeks later, Cedar Hollow gathers at the bakery to dedicate a small plaque to Rose Doyle and to name a new pastry after her, and Maggie finally adds her own handwritten card to the recipe box beside her mother's. As Nate leans in the doorway waiting to walk her to the festival planning meeting for next year, Maggie closes the box knowing the bakery, and her mother's name, are finally hers to keep.

copy_kdp.sottotitolo: A Cozy Bakery Mystery of Secrets, Sabotage, and a Killer Recipe
copy_kdp.descrizione:
Maggie Doyle came home to save her mother's bakery, not to solve a murder.

Six months after her mother's death, Maggie has poured every dollar and every ounce of hope into reopening Sweetbriar Bakery before Founder's Day, the one morning the whole town turns out. But when she opens the proofing drawer to check her sourdough, she finds Harold Pruitt, president of the Founder's Day Committee, stone cold and very dead.

The sheriff's suspicion turns to certainty when he pulls a recipe card from Harold's pocket, written in handwriting Maggie would know anywhere: her mother's.

Now the whole town is asking the same question. Did Maggie Doyle come home to bake, or to finish something her mother started?

With her business, her reputation, and possibly her freedom on the line, Maggie has one week to prove her innocence before Founder's Day ends in handcuffs instead of a ribbon cutting. Between batches of cinnamon rolls and increasingly uncomfortable visits from the sheriff, she starts digging through the town's oldest secrets and discovers that Pruitt was not nearly as beloved as his obituary will claim.

Everyone in Maple Hollow has a motive. Everyone has a recipe box full of secrets. And somebody is willing to let Maggie take the fall for a murder that started long before she ever came home.

Perfect for fans of small town bakeries, found family, and mysteries with a side of frosting.
